content: Essential laboratory equipment includes scales, centrifuges, vortex mixers, pH meters, water baths, refrigerators, freezers, and fume cupboards. While the specific analytical equipment required may vary depending on local needs and circumstances, certain fundamental instruments should be available to perform techniques such as colorimetry, spectrophotometry, and thin-layer chromatography. These may be housed in local hospital laboratories if necessary. Additional simple analytical techniques and instruments for rapid screening are also discussed below. Advanced analytical techniques, such as immunoassays, gas chromatography, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), atomic absorption spectrophotometry, and mass spectrometry, require specialized support, including servicing, spare parts, and consumables. Expertise in both the operation and maintenance of such equipment is critical. It is recommended that investment in and use of these advanced instruments be undertaken only as part of a comprehensive development program for analytical facilities. Table 1 provides examples of the types of analytical equipment that might be used in a toxicology laboratory. For instance, a spectrophotometer can be employed for initial screening of unknown substances, while rapid immunoassays and simple color tests (colorimetry) are also valuable tools. Portable anodic stripping voltammetry devices are useful for point-of-care measurements of blood lead concentrations. Blood gas analyzers equipped with pulse co-oximeters are widely available and can measure substances that cause metabolic acidosis. Certified reference standards for a range of analytes, such as controlled drugs, pesticides, and other chemicals, are essential for any analytical toxicology service. These standards are used to validate analytical methods and calibrate instruments. They can be purchased from chemical suppliers, included in commercial kits, or obtained from other laboratories, either locally or internationally. In cases where no reference standards are available (e.g., for new psychoactive substances), laboratories may need to develop new analytical methods, which can be formally validated later when standards become available. A variety of reagents and consumables are required depending on the assays offered by the laboratory. These may include solvents, purified water, and gases, as well as consumables like pipette tips, chromatography columns, and injection syringes. Replacement parts, such as detector lamps, must also be stocked. Ensuring a reliable supply of consumables is critical, particularly in resource-limited settings, to prevent stock shortages from becoming a limiting factor. Annex 2 provides a list of reference books on laboratory investigations. Decisions regarding which assays to offer in a toxicology laboratory depend on the local pattern of poisoning, the need for therapeutic drug monitoring, and the availability of equipment and trained staff. Laboratories must also consider whether they can provide a 24-hour service. Certain assays, such as those for carboxyhemoglobin, methaemoglobin, iron, lithium, toxic alcohols (e.g., methanol, ethanol, ethylene glycol), formate, paracetamol, salicylate, and paraquat, are frequently needed urgently to guide clinical management and should ideally be available in all hospitals treating poisoned patients. Less frequently requested assays, such as those for cholinesterase, lead, mercury, methotrexate, thallium, and general toxicology screens, may be offered by specialized toxicology laboratories. The clinical utility of these assays depends on the proximity of the laboratory to the treating hospital and the speed of sample transport and result reporting. Point-of-care testing refers to diagnostic testing performed near the patient to obtain results within minutes. These tests require minimal sample manipulation and can be conducted by personnel without formal laboratory training. Examples include qualitative urine drug screening tests using dipsticks or cassettes, blood lead concentration measurements from venous or capillary samples, cholinesterase activity testing from finger-prick samples, ethanol intoxication diagnosis using breath alcohol tests, and the use of pulse co-oximeters for measuring carboxyhemoglobin and methaemoglobin. While these tests are useful for screening and provisional diagnosis, laboratory confirmation should be sought when possible. Regular calibration, maintenance, and quality checks of point-of-care devices are essential. Analytical results must be interpreted in the context of the patient’s clinical status, exposure history, treatment provided, and other pathological conditions that may influence the results (e.g., renal or liver dysfunction). The roles of the analytical toxicologist and the clinical toxicologist at the poison center are critical in this process. A robust quality management system is essential to ensure the reliability of laboratory data. This system integrates all aspects of laboratory operations, including organizational structure, processes, procedures, and resources, to deliver high-quality services. Quality assurance focuses on processes and procedures, such as documentation, standard operating procedures (SOPs), instrument maintenance, calibration records, and validation methods. Quality control involves error control in test performance and verification of test results, with internal and external quality assessment components. Internal quality control typically involves analyzing control materials with known analyte concentrations, while external quality control involves blind test samples sent by an external agency. Participation in quality assurance and control programs is crucial for maintaining good analytical performance. Further guidance on quality management can be found in the WHO handbook on laboratory quality management systems. Compliance with recognized quality standards, such as ISO 15189 and ISO 17025, is recommended for analytical toxicology laboratories. Accreditation by an independent agency provides assurance of technical competence and integrity. Laboratories may also require licensure to store or use controlled substances, depending on national legal requirements. Laboratory safety is a key component of quality management. Staff must adhere to safety policies and procedures to mitigate risks associated with handling hazardous reagents and biological samples. Preventive measures include up-to-date staff vaccinations, treating all samples as high-risk, and providing decontamination and eye-wash facilities. Personal protective equipment, such as lab coats, gloves, and eye protection, must always be used. Staffing requirements depend on the volume and type of tests performed. Every analytical toxicology laboratory should have at least one experienced analytical toxicologist, with additional staff to cover absences. Laboratory technical staff should have a science education and practical laboratory experience. Training should be competency-based and documented in personal training logs. A career structure should be provided to retain trained staff and encourage knowledge transfer. Training for central analytical toxicology services must be tailored to the country’s context. It should be viewed as a continuous process to ensure staff competence and the delivery of high-quality services.
